title: Window Functions: Eliminate the Sort
description: A ROW_NUMBER window sorts the whole table; an index matching its PARTITION BY / ORDER BY supplies the order with no Sort. Why it matters: window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, running totals) are increasingly common in modern application code, and matching the supporting index to the window is a high-leverage, underused optimization.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
Window functions like `ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()`, and running-total `SUM() OVER (...)` have become a normal part of everyday SQL — they let you number rows, rank things, or compute a running total without writing a self-join or a correlated subquery. But there's a hidden requirement behind every one of them that a lot of developers never think about: to number or rank rows correctly, SQL Server has to see the rows in a very specific order first. If you write `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate)`, you're asking SQL Server to group the rows by customer, and within each customer's group, walk through their orders from earliest to latest, numbering them 1, 2, 3 as it goes. That's a completely reasonable thing to ask for — but the engine can only walk through rows 'in order' if the rows actually arrive in that order in the first place.

Think of it like being handed a shoebox full of receipts from many different customers, all mixed together in random order, and being asked to number each customer's receipts from oldest to newest. The only sane way to do that reliably is to first sort the whole box: group all of one customer's receipts together, and within each group put them in date order. Only then can you walk through the sorted pile and write '1, 2, 3...' on each one. That sorting step is exactly what SQL Server has to do when nothing about the table already presents the data in `(CustomerId, OrderDate)` order — it reads all the rows off the clustered index (which is very likely ordered by something else entirely, like `OrderId`), dumps them into a work area, and performs an explicit **Sort** operation before it can even begin numbering.

This Sort is what's called a **blocking operator**: unlike operators that can start producing output row by row as data streams past (like a simple filter), a Sort has to receive every single input row before it can produce its very first output row, because it has no way of knowing there isn't a smaller/later value still coming later in the input. For 300,000 rows, that means SQL Server has to hold a huge amount of data in memory (or spill it to disk) before the window function ever gets to do its actual job. SQL Server estimates how much memory this sort will need ahead of time and requests a **memory grant** for it; if that estimate is wrong (which happens more than you'd think, especially with skewed data or stale statistics) and the actual data doesn't fit, the excess data gets written out to **tempdb** — SQL Server's shared scratch-space database — as temporary files on disk. Reading and writing disk pages is dramatically slower than working entirely in memory, so a 'spill to tempdb' can turn what should be a fast, in-memory sort into a query that's crawling through disk I/O, and because tempdb is shared across the whole SQL Server instance, a big spill from one query can even slow down other, unrelated queries running at the same time by consuming shared tempdb I/O and space.

Here's the part that makes this an especially valuable lesson: this entire Sort step is completely avoidable, and the fix does not touch the query's T-SQL at all. If you build an index whose key columns exactly match the window's partitioning and ordering — partition column(s) first, then the order-by column(s), so `(CustomerId, OrderDate)` — then the index itself is already stored on disk in exactly the order the window function needs. SQL Server's optimizer is smart enough to recognize this: instead of scanning the table in whatever order it's stored and then sorting, it can simply read straight down the matching index, and the rows will already arrive in perfect partition-then-order sequence. The window function can then process them in a single streaming pass, numbering or ranking as it goes, with the Sort operator disappearing from the plan entirely. No blocking, no big memory grant, no risk of a tempdb spill — just a smooth, single pass over pre-sorted data.

Why does this matter so much in production? Because window functions today show up constantly in exactly the pattern that needs this fix: keyset/'seek' pagination (numbering rows so the app can request 'page 40'), 'gaps and islands' problems (finding runs of consecutive values or dates), deduplication (`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1` to grab 'the latest row per key'), and running totals or moving averages in financial or reporting queries. Every one of these patterns has this exact same sorting requirement lurking underneath it, and every one of them can be dramatically sped up — sometimes by an order of magnitude — by simply matching an index to the window specification. It's one of the highest-leverage, most underused optimizations in SQL Server, precisely because the query itself doesn't change at all; only the supporting index does. When you look at an execution plan for a slow window-function query, the signature to watch for is an explicit **Sort** operator sitting directly between the table/index scan and the window operator (which usually shows up as **Segment** and **Sequence Project**, or **Window Aggregate** depending on SQL Server version) — and the fix is to check whether an index already matches that Sort's columns, and if not, to build one that does.

## Scenario
`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate)` numbers each customer's orders chronologically over all 300,000 rows. The plan scans the clustered index and then performs an explicit **Sort** before the window operator.

## Why it's slow
A window function's `PARTITION BY` + `ORDER BY` requires its input to arrive ordered by exactly those columns — here `(CustomerId, OrderDate)`. Nothing provides that order, so SQL Server injects a **blocking Sort**: it must buffer and sort the entire input before emitting a single row. On large inputs that Sort needs a big memory grant and **spills to tempdb** when the grant is too small, adding disk I/O to what should be a streaming operation.

## What to look for
- An explicit **Sort** operator between the scan and the window (Segment / Sequence Project or Window Aggregate).
- The Sort's ordering columns match the window's `PARTITION BY` + `ORDER BY`.

## The concept
Build an index whose key **matches the window specification**: partition columns first, then order columns — `(CustomerId, OrderDate)`. The optimizer reads the already-ordered index and streams it straight into the window operator, so the **Sort disappears** entirely. This is one of the highest-leverage tricks for paging, gaps-and-islands, and running-total queries.
startingQuery: SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate) AS rn FROM Orders;
hints: The window's PARTITION BY / ORDER BY forces a specific input ordering; where does that ordering come from today?
With no matching index the engine must add a blocking Sort before it can number the rows.
Create an index keyed (CustomerId, OrderDate) -- partition column first, then the order column -- to match the window exactly.
